h1: Pacific Jade hops for black pepper and citrus notes
title: Pacific Jade Hops for Pepper and Citrus | Craft Beer School
desc: Pacific Jade hops explained: the New Zealand high alpha hop with black pepper, citrus and herbal notes, its soft bitterness and a homebrew saison idea.
teaser: Pacific Jade bitters hard and adds black pepper. In a saison or a peppery pale ale, that is a gift.
standfirst: Pacific Jade is a New Zealand high alpha hop with black pepper, citrus and fresh herbal notes. It bitters smoothly and has more character than most bittering hops. Here is how to use it at home.
sections:
Pacific Jade is a New Zealand variety grown in the Nelson region of the South Island. It was released in the 2000s as a high alpha hop.

Alpha acid usually runs from about 12 to 14%. Brewers describe its bitterness as soft for that alpha level. The aroma has black pepper, citrus and fresh herbs, with a bright, slightly lemony edge.
A bittering hop with a personality

Most high alpha hops are bought for clean bitterness and little else. Pacific Jade adds character even from the bittering slot. A 60 minute addition leaves a faint peppery note in the finish. Late additions bring out more citrus and fresh pepper.

For a 20 litre pale ale at 35 IBU, using Pacific Jade at 13% alpha for a 60 minute addition with 25% utilisation:

grams = 35 x 20 / (0.13 x 0.25 x 1,000) = about 22 g.

That small dose is a lot of bitterness. Weigh it on a scale that reads single grams.

Saison yeast produces peppery, spicy phenols on its own. Pacific Jade adds its own pepper and citrus. Together they make a saison that tastes deliberately spicy and dry.

Here is a 20 litre saison at about OG 1.052 and 30 IBU:

  • Pilsner malt 4.3 kg (88%).
  • Wheat malt 0.39 kg (8%).
  • Munich malt 0.2 kg (4%).
  • Pacific Jade 15 g at 60 minutes for about 24 IBU.
  • Pacific Jade 10 g at 10 minutes for about 6 IBU and pepper.
  • Pacific Jade 30 g at flameout.

Mash at 63 to 64 °C for a dry beer. Ferment with a saison yeast, starting around 20 °C and letting it rise.
The floor detail: saison yeast likes warmth

Saison is one of the few styles where Indian heat can help. Many saison strains ferment well into the upper 20s °C and finish very dry. A fermenter in a warm corner can work in the beer's favour.

The catch is control. A saison that starts at 30 °C may produce harsh fusel alcohols. Start cooler, around 20 °C, for the first two days. Then let it rise. The yeast finishes the job without the solvent edge.

It also suits:

  • Pale ales, where pepper and citrus give a savoury edge.
  • Pilsners and lagers, as a bittering hop with a light lift.
  • Beers with spices, especially black pepper or long pepper, where it doubles up.

For a woody, earthy bitterness in a steam beer instead, compare it with Northern Brewer. If you want caramel sweetness under the pepper, read about crystal malt colour first.

A peppery, citrusy pale ale or saison pairs well with Indian food that leans on black pepper, such as Chettinad chicken or pepper fry. The pepper in the beer meets the pepper in the dish. The carbonation and dryness help cut through oil. Keep bitterness moderate for spicy food. High bitterness and chilli heat amplify each other.
A single hop pale ale to learn it

Before using Pacific Jade in a saison, try it in a simple pale ale where nothing else competes. A 20 litre batch with 4.2 kg of pale malt, about 20 g of Pacific Jade at 60 minutes, 20 g at 10 minutes and 40 g at flameout gives a clear picture of what it does. Ferment clean with an American ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C.

Taste it fresh. Note where the pepper sits (in the aroma or the finish) and how the citrus compares with a familiar hop like Cascade. Then you will know how much to use when a saison yeast adds its own spice on top.

Pacific Jade shows up in Indian homebrew catalogues from time to time. Buy sealed foil packs, check the harvest year and freeze them. Its bitterness lasts better than its aroma. An older pack still bitters but loses some of the fresh pepper and citrus.

If it is unavailable, Magnum or another clean high alpha hop covers bittering. For the pepper, add a small late dose of a spicy noble hop like Saaz.

Two hops at the same IBU can taste very different, because bitterness quality depends on the alpha acid types, the oils that survive the boil and the beer around them. Why Pacific Jade tastes soft at 13% alpha is the kind of question that makes recipe design predictable.
faqs: What does Pacific Jade taste like?
Black pepper, citrus and fresh herbs. The bitterness is generally considered soft for its alpha acid.
What is the alpha acid of Pacific Jade?
Usually around 12 to 14%. Use the lot analysis to calculate exact weights.
Saisons, pale ales and lagers, plus spiced beers where black pepper fits the recipe.
